Amoxicillin Trihydrate: Aminopenicillin (beta-lactam antibiotic); Clavulanate Potassium: Beta-lactamase inhibitor
Schedule H – prescription only; Clavulanate Potassium: Schedule H – prescription only
sections: White crystalline powder (trihydrate), slightly soluble in water.
White to off-white hygroscopic crystalline powder (potassium salt), freely soluble in water.

Amoxicillin Trihydrate: The second aminopenicillin after ampicillin; on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and one of the most prescribed antibiotics worldwide. First approval/introduction: Discovered 1958; introduced 1972 (Beecham Research Laboratories); US 1974. Clavulanate Potassium: The first clinically used beta-lactamase inhibitor; on the WHO List of Essential Medicines in combination with amoxicillin. First approval/introduction: Discovered 1974–75 from Streptomyces clavuligerus (Beecham); amoxicillin–clavulanate launched 1981 (UK).
Amoxicillin 500 mg + Clavulanate 125 mg; Amoxicillin 875 mg + Clavulanate 125 mg

Amoxicillin Trihydrate Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking, causing bacterial lysis (bactericidal). Receptor / target profile: Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking, causing bacterial lysis.

Clavulanate Potassium Irreversibly inhibits many plasmid- and chromosomally-mediated beta-lactamases, protecting amoxicillin from hydrolysis and extending its spectrum to beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus (MSSA), E. coli, Klebsiella and anaerobes. Receptor / target profile: Mechanism-based ('suicide') irreversible inhibitor of many class A beta-lactamases.
Summary: Bioavailability ~70–90%; Tmax 1–2 h. ~18% protein bound. Excreted largely unchanged in urine. Half-life ~1 h.
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax ~1 h. ~25% protein bound. Hepatic metabolism and renal excretion. Half-life ~1 h.
